  • Age (OR = 0.96): among passengers of the same sex and class, each additional year of age multiplies the odds of survival by 0.96, i.e. decreases them by about 4%.

As in section 3, odds ratios are hard to compare between variables. Predicted probabilities (or AMEs) are clearer. Here’s the AME of each predictor, using marginaleffects:

library(marginaleffects)
avg_comparisons(m8)

The results:

  • being a man rather than a woman: −47 percentage points of probability of survival (holding class and age constant);
  • being in 3rd class rather than 1st: −42 percentage points (holding sex and age constant);
  • each additional year of age: −0.5 percentage points (holding sex and class constant).

How to say it:

✅ “Holding class and age constant, being a man (rather than a woman) is associated with a probability of survival 47 percentage points lower (p < 0.001). Holding sex and age constant, being in 3rd class (rather than 1st) is associated with a probability 42 percentage points lower (p < 0.001). Holding sex and class constant, each additional year of age is associated with a probability about 0.5 points lower (p < 0.001).”

Three honest sentences, three real findings.

5.3 Reading coefficients from a multiple regression

Three rules that always apply.

Rule 1: always add “holding the other variables constant” when you interpret a coefficient. Each coefficient answers a specific question: “if I compare two people who are identical on all the other variables, but who differ on this one, how much does the outcome differ?”. That’s a very different question from the one answered by a simple regression (“how much does the outcome differ between people who differ on this variable, period?”). Mixing the two is one of the most common mistakes in applied statistics.

Rule 2: a coefficient can change — in size, in significance, even in sign — when you add or remove other variables. We just saw it with age and fare: +0.35 alone, −0.51 after adding class. This is not a glitch, and it’s not that one of the two is “right” and the other “wrong”. They answer different questions. Which one you report depends on what you want to know (section 5.4).

Rule 3: don’t compare coefficient sizes across different units. In m7, the coefficient of Age (−0.51) is much smaller than that of Class3rd class (−81.4). This doesn’t mean class matters more than age: age is in years, class is a 0/1 jump between categories, and 0.51 £ per year × 60 years = 30 £, almost half of the class effect. To compare the importance of variables measured on different scales, use predicted probabilities, AMEs, or standardize the variables first (we won’t cover that here).

5.4 Confounds, controls, and the problem of “controlling for everything”

Let’s pose a new question: did paying a higher fare, in itself, improve a passenger’s chance of surviving? We saw in section 3 that yes, more expensive tickets came with higher survival. But why? There are at least two possible stories:

  • Story A: fare itself helped survival — maybe it bought you something concrete, like a cabin close to the lifeboats, or priority in the evacuation.
  • Story B: fare had no direct effect at all. Expensive tickets came with 1st class, and 1st class is what actually mattered — being on the upper decks, being evacuated first, etc. Fare just happened to be a label for class.

The simple regression glm(Survived ~ Fare) can’t tell these two apart. Let’s add class and see what happens:

m_fare       = glm(Survived ~ Fare, family = binomial, data = data)
m_fare_class = glm(Survived ~ Fare + Class, family = binomial, data = data)

library(marginaleffects)
avg_comparisons(m_fare,       variables = list(Fare = 10))

 Estimate Std. Error    z Pr(>|z|)    S  2.5 % 97.5 %
   0.0338    0.00457 7.41   <0.001 42.8 0.0249 0.0428

Term: Fare
Type: response
Comparison: +10
avg_comparisons(m_fare_class, variables = list(Fare = 10))

 Estimate Std. Error    z Pr(>|z|)   S   2.5 % 97.5 %
   0.0144    0.00505 2.86  0.00425 7.9 0.00454 0.0244

Term: Fare
Type: response
Comparison: +10

The AMEs for +10 £:

  • Without class: +3.4 percentage points of survival per 10 £. That’s the raw effect we reported in section 3.
  • Controlling for class: +1.4 percentage points per 10 £. The effect shrinks to less than half.

So most of what looked like “fare helping survival” was actually “class helping survival”. Among passengers in the same class, paying 10 £ more is only associated with a tiny 1.4-point gain. Class was doing most of the work, and fare was taking the credit.

What just happened: a confound

Class is a confound for the relationship between fare and survival. A confound is a variable that is a common cause of both the predictor and the outcome:

  • class influences fare (1st class tickets are expensive, 3rd class tickets are cheap);
  • class influences survival (1st class passengers were evacuated first).

Because of this double link, class creates a spurious statistical association between fare and survival, on top of any direct effect fare may have. The simple regression lumps the two together. The multiple regression, by controlling for class, isolates the direct effect of fare.

Drawing the problem: DAGs

To think clearly about confounding, researchers draw small diagrams called DAGs (Directed Acyclic Graphs). Each variable is a box, and each arrow means “causally influences”. Our situation looks like this:

            Class
           /     \
          v       v
        Fare ---> Survived (direct effect, if any)

There are two paths from Fare to Survived:

  • the direct path: Fare → Survived (what we care about: does paying more, in itself, help?);
  • the back-door path: Fare ← Class → Survived (the confounding path, through class).

The simple regression mixes both. Controlling for class blocks the back-door path, leaving only the direct one.

The rule of thumb: a confound is a variable that influences both the predictor you care about and the outcome. If you don’t control for it, the coefficient of your predictor absorbs the confound’s effect. If you do control for it, the coefficient reflects only the direct effect.

“Controlling for” a variable

Controlling for a variable just means: adding it to the regression. By doing so, we ask the model to compare only observations that have the same value on this variable. In m_fare_class, controlling for class means: “compare the survival rates of passengers who paid different fares, but within each class”. This neutralizes the class pathway.

Why not just add every variable as a control?

This is the trap. It feels safe (“the more controls, the better”), but it isn’t. We’ll elaborate all this later, but for now, you can apply this heuristic. When deciding whether you want to include a variable as a control, ask yourself this:

Is it a plausible common cause of my predictor and my outcome?

→ If yes, it’s a confound, control for it. If not, don’t.

NB: Causal inference is a whole field of its own, and this is only the first chapter. The main thing to remember: regression doesn’t automatically give you causal effects, even when you add controls.

6. Correlation

A correlation coefficient (r) measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two continuous variables, on a scale from −1 to +1:

  • +1: perfect positive relationship (all dots exactly on an upward line);
  • 0: no linear relationship;
  • −1: perfect negative relationship (all dots exactly on a downward line).

cor.test() computes it, along with a p-value and a confidence interval:

cor.test(data$Age, data$Fare)

    Pearson's product-moment correlation

data:  data$Age and data$Fare
